sessions.title: [TEST] CPR-49 Dry Run: Sequencing Velantumab in KRAS G12C NSCLC
sessions.transcriptText:
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Good evening everyone, and welcome. I'm Priya Nandakumar, and I'll be moderating tonight's Community Health Media program on sequencing velantumab in previously
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: treated KRAS G12C mutant non-small cell lung cancer. We'll have about thirty minutes of discussion with our faculty, and then we'll save
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: time for Q&A at the end, so please drop your questions in the Q&A box as we go.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: I'm joined by Dr. Marcus Hale, a thoracic medical oncologist at Brightwater Cancer Center, and Dr. Elena Varga, who directs the lung
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: cancer program at Northlake University Medical Center. Welcome to you both.
Dr. Marcus Hale: Thanks Priya, glad to be here.
Dr. Elena Varga: Thank you, it's a pleasure.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Marcus, let's start with the data. For people who haven't followed it closely, what did HORIZON-L2 actually show?
Dr. Marcus Hale: So HORIZON-L2 was the randomized phase three trial of velantumab versus docetaxel in patients whose disease had progressed after a platinum doublet
Dr. Marcus Hale: and immunotherapy. Um, the headline was a progression-free survival benefit, a median of about six point eight months versus four point one,
Dr. Marcus Hale: and the hazard ratio was around zero point six. Overall survival is still maturing, and that's an important caveat. Response rates were
Dr. Marcus Hale: roughly forty percent versus fourteen percent with docetaxel.
Dr. Marcus Hale: What struck me most was the durability in the responders. When patients responded, the median duration of response was close to ten
Dr. Marcus Hale: months, which you just don't see with docetaxel in this setting.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Elena, does that change what you do on Monday morning?
Dr. Elena Varga: It does, with some nuance. For a patient with a confirmed KRAS G12C mutation who has progressed on chemo immunotherapy and has
Dr. Elena Varga: a reasonable performance status, velantumab is now my preferred second line option. The nuance is in who we're testing and how fast.
Dr. Elena Varga: If we don't have the KRAS result back when the patient progresses, we end up defaulting to docetaxel, and that's a missed
Dr. Elena Varga: opportunity.
Dr. Elena Varga: So honestly the biggest practice change for our group wasn't the drug, it was making sure broad next generation sequencing is ordered
Dr. Elena Varga: at diagnosis and not at progression. We moved to reflex testing on every non-squamous specimen, and we added plasma testing when tissue
Dr. Elena Varga: is going to take more than two weeks.
Dr. Marcus Hale: I'd echo that. In the community, the turnaround time is the real bottleneck. We've had patients wait three or four weeks for
Dr. Marcus Hale: tissue results. Running liquid biopsy in parallel has cut that down to about a week for most of our patients.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Let's talk about toxicity, because that's what I hear the most questions about. What should people expect?
Dr. Marcus Hale: The two things to watch are hepatotoxicity and diarrhea. Transaminase elevations were seen in about a third of patients in HORIZON-L2, and
Dr. Marcus Hale: grade three or higher in around eight percent. They tend to show up in the first six to eight weeks. So we
Dr. Marcus Hale: check liver function tests every two weeks for the first two months, then monthly.
Dr. Marcus Hale: Diarrhea is usually low grade and manageable with loperamide, but you have to set expectations up front. I tell every patient: call
Dr. Marcus Hale: us on day one, not day four.
Dr. Elena Varga: And there's one interaction that matters. Patients who had immunotherapy recently seem to have a higher risk of liver toxicity, especially if
Dr. Elena Varga: the last dose was within about six weeks. So we're careful about timing, and some of us will wait a few extra
Dr. Elena Varga: weeks after the last checkpoint inhibitor dose before starting, if the disease allows it.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: That's a really practical point. How do you manage dose reductions?
Dr. Elena Varga: We follow the label reductions, but I'd say we're quicker to hold and re-challenge at a lower dose than we used to
Dr. Elena Varga: be. In our experience, most patients who have a grade two liver signal can come back at the reduced dose and stay
Dr. Elena Varga: on therapy. Stopping permanently at the first sign of toxicity probably leaves benefit on the table.
Dr. Marcus Hale: Agreed. The other piece is the nurse navigator. Our nurse calls every patient at day ten and day twenty-one. That one change
Dr. Marcus Hale: has kept more people on therapy than anything else we've done.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Where does velantumab fit if a patient has brain metastases?
Dr. Marcus Hale: There's some intracranial activity, but the trial excluded untreated or symptomatic brain metastases, so the data are limited. For small, asymptomatic lesions
Dr. Marcus Hale: I'll use it and image closely. For anything symptomatic, I'm treating the brain locally first.
Dr. Elena Varga: Same approach. I'd also say we need a dedicated study in that population, because it's common in KRAS G12C disease and we're
Dr. Elena Varga: extrapolating.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Before we turn to the audience, give me one takeaway each.
Dr. Marcus Hale: Test everyone at diagnosis, and run plasma in parallel if tissue is slow. You can't use the drug if you don't know
Dr. Marcus Hale: the mutation.
Dr. Elena Varga: Anticipate the liver toxicity and build the monitoring into your workflow before you start the first patient. Hold, reduce and re-challenge rather
Dr. Elena Varga: than stopping.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Great. Let's open it up for questions from the audience. We have quite a few coming in.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: The first one is from a community oncologist. They ask: if a patient progressed on immunotherapy alone, without chemotherapy, would you still
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: use velantumab second line, or go to a platinum doublet first?
Dr. Marcus Hale: Good question, and that's outside the trial population. HORIZON-L2 required prior platinum. In that situation I'd still favor the platinum doublet second
Dr. Marcus Hale: line for most patients, and keep velantumab for third line, unless there's a reason they can't get chemotherapy.
Dr. Elena Varga: I'd agree, although for a frail patient who isn't a chemo candidate I'd be comfortable going straight to velantumab.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Next, from a nurse practitioner: how often do you check liver function, and do you hold for grade one elevations?
Dr. Marcus Hale: Every two weeks for eight weeks, then monthly. We don't hold for grade one, we just repeat sooner. Grade two we hold
Dr. Marcus Hale: until it comes back to grade one, then restart at the reduced dose.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: A pharmacist is asking about drug interactions, particularly acid reducing agents.
Dr. Elena Varga: Yes, proton pump inhibitors reduce absorption, so we try to avoid them. If a patient really needs acid suppression, we use an
Dr. Elena Varga: H2 blocker and separate the dosing by several hours. Our pharmacist reviews every medication list before the first dose.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Here's one about cost and access. A community oncologist in a rural practice says prior authorization has been taking two to three
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: weeks. Any tips?
Dr. Marcus Hale: Start the authorization the day the KRAS result comes back, not the day of progression. And use the manufacturer's bridge program while
Dr. Marcus Hale: you wait. We've had good luck with that.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Several people are asking the same thing: is there a role for velantumab in the first line setting?
Dr. Elena Varga: Not yet outside a trial. There are first line combination studies with immunotherapy underway, but given the liver signal we've seen with
Dr. Elena Varga: recent checkpoint inhibitor exposure, I'd want to see that safety data before using any combination.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: Last question, from a fellow: how do you talk to patients about the modest overall survival data so far?
Dr. Marcus Hale: I'm honest that we don't have the survival result yet. What we do know is that more patients respond, and the responses
Dr. Marcus Hale: last longer, with a side effect profile that's different from chemotherapy and, for most people, easier to live with. Most patients find
Dr. Marcus Hale: that a reasonable trade.
Dr. Elena Varga: And I'd add, framing it around what matters to the patient, whether that's time at home or avoiding hair loss or infusion
Dr. Elena Varga: visits, makes the conversation much easier.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: That's all the time we have. Thank you, Dr. Hale and Dr. Varga, and thank you all for joining. You'll get a
Dr. Priya Nandakumar: short survey after the program, and we'd really appreciate your feedback. Good night.
